lessons.title: Place value, ordering and rounding
lessons.summary: Use tenths and hundredths, order negative decimals and round to significant figures.
lessons.objective: Use tenths and hundredths, order negative decimals and round to significant figures.
lessons.before: Imagine cutting a length into tenths. A whole metre contains ten tenths.
lessons.ideas:
Multiplying by 0.1 divides by 10. Dividing by 0.1 multiplies by 10. Use 100 for hundredths.

Start at the first non-zero digit. Keep the required number of digits. Use the next digit to round and leave zeroes where they hold place value.

Compare the position on the number line. Moving left makes the value smaller even when its distance from zero grows.
lessons.method:
Use an inverse calculation to check the result.

Read the rounding instruction before you calculate.

Use a common decimal length when comparing close readings.
mistakes: A division does not always make a number smaller. Ask how many parts fit.
Ignore leading zeroes when counting significant digits. Keep place-holding zeroes such as in 3400.
A minus sign changes which size comparison gives the greater value.

examples.title: Dividing by a small decimal
examples.question:
A label shows a length of \(2.5\) m.

  1. Calculate \(2.5\) ÷ \(0.01\).

    [2]

  2. Calculate \(2.5\) × \(0.01\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) \(0.01\) is one of 100 equal parts of 1. Dividing counts how many of these parts fit.

Multiply both numbers in the division by 100. The divisor becomes 1.

\(250\)

(b) Multiplying by one tenth or one hundredth makes the value smaller. Move the digits to lower place values.

\(0.025\)

examples.title: Significant figures on a length label
examples.question:
A printed label records \(4.73\) cm.

  1. Write the length to two significant figures.

    [2]

  2. A separate measurement is \(4730\) mm. Round it to two significant figures.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Start at the first non-zero digit. Keep the units and tenths digits. Look at the hundredths digit of \(4.73\) before rounding.

The rounded length is \(4.7\) cm.

(b) For this four-digit measurement keep the thousands and hundreds digits. Replace dropped places by zero.

\(4700\) mm

examples.title: Comparing decimal readings
examples.question:
Two screen readings are \(-21.3\) and \(-21.38\).

  1. Write the lower reading.

    [2]

  2. Give the positive difference between the two readings.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Extra zeroes do not change a decimal. Compare \(-21.30\) with \(-21.38\) on a number line.

lessons.title: Signed calculations, powers and roots
lessons.summary: Apply the calculation order and explain sign rules for integers and powers.
lessons.objective: Apply the calculation order and explain sign rules for integers and powers.
lessons.before: Use gains and losses to picture the operation.
lessons.ideas:
Estimate with nearby friendly numbers to check the size. Then multiply or divide the magnitudes. Matching signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result.

Evaluate brackets first, then powers and roots. Multiply and divide, then add and subtract. Read equal-priority operations left to right.

For a common non-zero base, add exponents to multiply and subtract to divide. Dividing a power by itself gives a zero exponent and value 1.

The square of a negative number is positive. The square root symbol gives the non-negative root of a non-negative number. A negative number can have a negative cube root.
lessons.method:
Use the inverse operation to check the sign of a quotient.

Write one line for the bracket and a second line for the product.

Keep the base unchanged when giving the combined power.

Check a proposed root by raising it to the given power.
mistakes: Adding negatives has a different sign rule from multiplying negatives.
Addition does not come before multiplication unless brackets say so.
Do not add the exponents when adding the powers.
Solving an equation such as x² = 49 is different from finding the value of the square root symbol.

examples.title: Signed movements
examples.question:
Each move lowers a marker by 7 points. A game counts 3 moves.

  1. Calculate the overall change.

    [2]

  2. In a different rule, an adjustment of \(21\) is divided by \(-3\). Find the new adjustment.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each move is \(-7\). The magnitude of the change is \(7\times 3=21\). One negative factor gives a negative result.

\(-21\)

(b) A positive number divided by a negative number has a negative result. Use multiplication to check.

\(-7\)

examples.title: Calculate in the right order
examples.question:
An activity card shows \(19+2\times(2^2-3)\).

  1. Calculate its value.

    [2]

  2. Now calculate \((19+2)\times(2^2-3)\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Inside the bracket, calculate \(2^2=4\) first. The bracket becomes \(1\).

Next multiply \(1\) by 2. Then add 19.

\(21\)

(b) The first bracket changes the order. Complete both brackets before multiplying.

\(21\)

examples.title: Combining powers
examples.question:
An expression contains \(4^4\times 4^3\) and \(4^4\div 4^4\).

  1. Write the product as a power of 4. Give the power.

    [2]

  2. Find the value of the division expression.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The first power contains 4 copies of 4 multiplied together. The second contains 3.

The product therefore has \(4+3=7\) copies.

\(7\)

(b) Dividing a non-zero number by itself gives 1. Subtracting equal exponents also gives \(4^0=1\).

\(1\)

examples.title: Square and cube roots
examples.question:
One card shows \(9\). A second card shows \(-125\).

  1. Find \(\sqrt[3]{-125}\).

    [2]

  2. Give the two solutions of \(x^2=9\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Check by cubing. There are three negative factors in \((-5)^3=-125\), so the result is negative.

\(-5\)

(b) Both \(3^2=9\) and \((-3)^2=9\) have a positive product.

\(-3\) and \(3\)

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and number families
lessons.summary: Use common factors and multiples and classify whole and rational numbers.
lessons.objective: Use common factors and multiples and classify whole and rational numbers.
lessons.before: If every item must be used, each total must divide exactly by the number of groups.
lessons.ideas:
A factor divides a number exactly. To find the highest common factor, compare factor lists or use the common prime factors.

The lowest common multiple is the first positive number that is a multiple of both inputs.

The natural numbers are counting numbers. The integers include positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero. A rational number can be written as a fraction of integers with non-zero denominator.
lessons.method:
Check both divisions leave no remainder.

In a repeating event question, do not count the first meeting as the next one.

Use the smallest family that contains the number when asked.
mistakes: The highest common factor cannot be more than the smaller total.
The product is a common multiple but a smaller one may exist.
A written fraction can simplify to an integer. Check the value before classifying.

examples.title: Making identical activity packs
examples.question:
A class has 30 wooden counters and 30 card squares. All objects must be used.

  1. What is the greatest number of identical packs they can make?

    [2]

  2. How many objects are in each pack?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A possible pack count divides both 30 and 30 exactly.

The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. The greatest is \(30\).

\(30\)

(b) Each pack gets 1 counters and 1 squares.

Add the two parts of one pack.

\(2\)

examples.title: Two repeating bells
examples.question:
A workshop has bells that ring every 19 minutes and every 4 minutes. They ring together at opening.

  1. How many minutes later will they ring together again?

    [2]

  2. How many times does the 19-minute bell ring in that time, excluding the opening ring?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Write multiples of 19 and 4. The first positive number on both lists is 76.

\(76\) minutes

(b) Divide the elapsed time by the interval for this bell.

\(4\)

examples.title: Sorting number families
examples.question:
One tile shows \(-\frac{37}{4}\). Another tile shows \(-9\).

  1. Which is the smallest family containing \(-\frac{37}{4}\)?

    [2]

  2. Give the smallest number family containing \(-9\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) \(-\frac{37}{4}\) is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. The division has a remainder, so the value is not an integer.

Rational numbers

(b) A negative whole-number value is an integer. Every integer is also rational.

Integers
